old: Glass! I have put into a good many ports, my boy, and I never saw the like.
new: Glass! I have put in at many good ports, my boy, and I have never seen the like.¶The sailor might well say so.¶Only in late years had the fishermen of the north of Europe, in the cod fisheries of Norway, begun to buoy their great nets with globes of blown glass, which do not drink the water as cork does, and neither rot nor sink. They were still a novelty of the northern seas, and an American sailor had very likely never seen one.¶The sea opens strange roads to floating bodies. In the South Pacific the waters turn in a great round: up the coasts of Chile and Peru, westward below the line, then south, and back to the east under the westerly winds; and whatever falls into that round, a spar, a cask, a float, it carries for months and for years. The sea is patient, and sooner or later it brings in everything that it does not sink.

old: Pencroff might have told the rest then, by the fire. He did not. The sailor meant to go back and see, and to bring home with his own hands whatever he found, and lay it on the table before them all.
We had it, Pencroff, said Herbert. "For an hour."
new: Yes, answered Herbert; "and it lay under our hands the whole time the sea was out."
